description: Hi! My name is Shaurya Singh and I am a Senior at Hamilton Southeastern High School. My specialized field of study is Mathematical Modeling, a highly interdisciplinary craft that requires both technical skills and creativity. I hope to carry my experience with ML, Partial Differential Equations, Linear Algebra, and Statistics into the upcoming challenges!
summary:
Since 2000, MODIS has recorded fires and VIIRS since 2012 but due to significant differences between the two satellites the fire record will be significantly affected. As a result, there is an artificial “jump” in fires in 2012 when suddenly switching to use both.

We take real hotspot data from NASA FIRMS, then have both fit a 1km grid. We mark each square once per day for fire, however many pixels are lit up.
 
We use this to learn an “exchange rate” between the two satellites from the years both were flying, separately for each region and season, and use it to convert the MODIS-only years onto the VIIRS scale and make it comparable. 

Every month we converted comes with an uncertainty range to ensure reliability, and we tested the method on years it was never given. As a result, totals landed between 4 to 14% of what VIIRS actually recorded across 5 countries, in comparison to around 50% off for raw MODIS and the 2012 jump was gone.

We display the results on a world map, on a 3D model of Earth. Users can zoom in to see the hotspot levels for each cell in the grid. On the side, they are given metrics that show a month-by-year burning activity calendar from 2000 to 2025. It also shows anomalies against normal conditions, the typical fire season, year totals with uncertainty, and even a before/after chart to demonstrate the difference between the harmonized and non-harmonized data.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Our project makes the fire records of NASA’s two main satellites for data collection harmonized into a consistent history and record. Since 2000, MODIS has recorded fires and VIIRS since 2012 but due to significant differences between the two satellites the fire record will be significantly affected without some change. VIIRS is much higher resolution than MODIS (375m vs 1km respectively) meaning it picks up on much more minute detections. As a result, the aggregates of fire detection and Fire Radiative Power differ greatly. As a result, there is an artificial “jump” in fires in 2012 when VIIRS was introduced as it detected much more fires than MODIS did but didn’t reflect an overall changing trend.

We take real hotspot data from NASA FIRMS and keeps only vegetation fires that pass confidence checks to ensure we don’t account for false alarms. Then, we count fires by taking the data to fit a 1km grid and count fairly by marking each square once per day for fire, however many pixels are lit up.

 

We use this to learn an “exchange rate” between the two satellites from the years both were flying, separately for each region and season, and use it to convert the MODIS-only years onto the VIIRS scale and make it comparable. 

Every month we converted comes with an uncertainty range to ensure reliability, and we tested the method on years it was never given. As a result, totals landed between 1 to 14% of what VIIRS actually recorded across 10 countries, in comparison to around 50% off for raw MODIS and the 2012 jump was gone.

We display the results on a world map, on a 3D model of Earth. Users can switch between 2D and 3D models (with accessible colors), and can zoom in to see the hotspot levels for each cell in the grid. On the side, they are given metrics that show a month-by-year burning activity calendar from 2000 to 2025. It also shows anomalies against normal conditions, the typical fire season, year totals with uncertainty, and even a before/after chart to demonstrate the difference between the harmonized and non-harmonized data. Users can also look at burned-area layers, clickable provinces and counties, and draw their own areas to have graphs on. Users can download everything as CSV, PNG, or SVG in English or Spanish. Fire managers, responders, and scientists can then judge whether a season is truly unusual against 25 years of consistent history.

What benefits does it have? 

As with the problem outlined, the project was able to harmonize data from MODIS and VIIRS. Effectively, this allows them to keep the extensive historical record and trends of fires and hotspots instead of us having to throw out MODIS data.

Now, the complete switch to VIIRS from MODIS is easier now as it is in its final stages and another worry of decommissioning them is checked off. With NASA being able to have complete use of VIIRS, they have more accuracy with its higher resolution, detecting small fires better; better nighttime accuracy; better continuity as it is more consistent in pixel size along the swath of data collection; and faster data as VIIRS is near real-time.

With a preserved historical record, fire managers and researchers can better ensure that people are safe before fires even come to them. They will have greater predictive capability and risk modeling for hotspots and fires allowing us to better handle and have targeted land management, have better insurance and urban planning, and better track ecological and climate change. With faster, more real time data, they are able to have faster emergency responses, faster public alerts, safer evacuation planning, and smarter resource allocation.

What is the intended impact of the project? 

MODIS is near the end of its life and its orbit is now drifting. One of VIIRS satellites has stopped. MODIS’s data is the only link to fire history before 2012, so once it is decommissioned, the data from to overlap the two will be gone. Without harmonization, the first 12 years of satellite fire history cannot be compared with the data of today. Our tool allows that data to be preserved, so when someone asks if this season is unusual. They can compare it with 25 years of history instead of the 14 creating more concrete trends and anomalies. 

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? 

We built the data pipeline in Python. DuckDB runs quick SQL over millions of hotspot/fire records, Polars and PyArrow handle the tables and compact Parquet files, and NumPy runs the bootstrap uncertainty calculations. All of the data comes from NASA FIRMS active-fire records for the main method and NASA LP DAAC products accessed through Earthdata served as layers and research tests.

The web app itself is written in JS, HTML, and CSS. MapLibre GL draws the 3D globe and flat map, D3 and Observable Plot draws the charts, and a browser Parquet reader loads the data directly. Map imagery comes from the NASA GIBS Blue Marble and OpenStreetMap.

How is your project creative? 

Our project is creative because of our methodology in harmonization. One of the first things we realized as a team was that we as highschoolers under a small time limit, while creative, would not be more knowledgeable on this topic than NASA and CONAE researchers and especially not more novel. So, we looked towards existing efforts to bridge the gaps between MODIS and VIIRS, while not initially creative as we looked towards attempts at creating continuity between the two satellites with hotspots, we decided to look towards more “successful” attempts with other data sources.

The Cloud Mask, Land Surface Temperature, and Vegetation Indices were all different projects that relied on both MODIS and VIIRS satellites and were largely successful. Our creativity came through here, as we investigated the methods used with these and applied them to the normalization in the data (resolution, timings, capture angle, etc.). Not only that, we came up with methods to make the two satellites comparable so a trend could be made to transform pre-VIIRS data by analyzing how these projects did so.

In addition, we wanted to take a slightly different route in what we focused on compared to what we thought others would do. Rather than focusing on maximizing the comparability/harmonization of each hotspot/point, we wanted to focus on trends. The reason for this was that the original challenge wanted harmonization so we could preserve historical trends, so we wanted to make sure the trends were best comparable to VIIRS rather than each hotspot/point as an individual.

With this approach, we wanted to split the year up into seasons and even categorize fires. The reason for this is that we could track regional trends exceptionally well if we accounted for the seasons; in addition, if we categorized fires we would have a more fair product as we would not be treating all fires equally. The importance of the second consideration is obvious when you consider that large-scale recurring fires due to slash-and-burn farming are different to forest fires (though some forest fires are regular and necessary for ecosystems to thrive). Admittedly, the categorization of fires hurt the accuracy and we had to remove it despite its creativity.

What factors did your team consider?

We considered the difference in overpass times between MODIS and VIIRS and the daily fire cycle. We also considered the region and seasons, and differences between areas to create a formula for the harmonizing trend between the two satellites to create our map. We also considered false detections that come from volcanoes, gas flares and industry, which will create low-confidence VIIRS points. Due to our focus on mapping regional trends and seasons, our program is strongest for regional trends nad single small cell-months are rough estimates in a range.

We also considered accessibility that our users may encounter, utilizing colourblind-safe colours for our map.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS active fire data (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m)
